name: Southern Ocean Surf Reef ("Midds Reef")
year: Quarry establishment from ~Oct 2024 [R17]; first rock placed on the seabed 18 Mar 2025 (planned six weeks) [R26][R30]; 'more than two-thirds complete' 16 May 2025, finish pushed to mid-June [R27]; storm of Mon 26 May 2025 moved some core rock [R25][R28]; officially opened 16 July 2025 'after four months of work' [R29][R31][R1][R2]. The City's programme 'Jan-Mar 2025, practical completion Mar 2025' [R3][R32] was a plan, not what happened.
type: Submerged rock-berm surf reef, 62,800 t of layered granite per the City's design table (belly, core, Class 1 armour) [R3] (the ~70,000 t quoted by The Inertia [R6] is kept as a rounded journalistic figure), no geotextile [R2][R3][R1] Tonnage note (audit 2026-10-10): the City design table gives 62,800 t [R3]; the ~70,000 t of The Inertia [R6] is a rounded journalistic figure; both kept, the design table is preferred.
purpose: Surfing amenity / tourism / youth retention - the reef's sole and primary stated design objective; unlike most artificial surf reefs, coastal erosion protection was not a driver [R3][R8][R9]
size: Length 165 m; width up to 110 m; crest at -1.0 m AHD; total volume 62,800 t (belly D50 0.16 m/12,400 t, core D50 0.49 m/23,600 t, armour D50 0.94 m/26,800 t); reef sits ~140 m offshore [R3] Shape model (07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/HANDOFF.md section 3; HIGH confidence for position, size, orientation): default outline = Bluecoast final-design outermost contour [R3], placed on the Esri 2026-01-20 image by a fitted wedge (IoU 0.84); area 13,104 m2; along/across the crest 164.6 / 121.2 m (the card's 'width up to 110 m' is the design crest length at -2 m AHD, not the outline width); nearest edge 66.8 m from the beach-face line (the card's '~140 m offshore' is the City's value from an undefined reference, 'landward toe'; not reconciled). Volume about 34,000 m3 (DERIVED: 62,800 t [R3] divided by an assumed rock bulk density of 1.85 t/m3, ASSUMPTION of the shape agent with no source, 07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/HANDOFF.md section 3; the ~70,000 t of [R6] would give about 37,800 m3 by the same density). Crest levels are design values in AHD [R3], not surveyed; no as-built survey was found (negative search result of this project). The City's own design table (registry img-10, read again 2026-10-10) states 'Reef volume 34,000 m3 (based on 2017 bathymetry)' [R3], so the volume above is no longer only DERIVED: the table value and the tonnage-over-density value agree to within rounding. Seabed and water depth under the reef (3D model, LOW confidence, 07_scale/shapes/southern-ocean-surf-reef-albany/3d/METHODS_3D.md sections 3.2 and 4): about -2.1 m AHD at the shoreward apex to -7.4 m AHD at the offshore toe, DERIVED from the depth contours of the 2015 RHDHV Option B plan [R21] (datum not printed; read as AHD, georeferenced by hand); a 2018 BMT sounding of 2.7 m below chart datum near the shore is about 1.6 m deeper than that profile if chart datum equals AHD [R20] (unresolved). Update 2026-10-13 (Lior uploads, agent Albany uploads): Rock mass: the City's table gives 62,800 t [R3]; ABC and The Inertia say 70,000 t of granite [R2][R6]; Raised Water Research says 'more than 47,000 m3 (70,000 tonnes)', footprint 1.61 ha, 'designed 140-375 m offshore' and a crest 'roughly .75 m under the surface at low tide', mixing 2015 and final-design values with no source [R10][R23]. Distance offshore: 140 m [R3][R26] (City news of 7 Mar 2025) vs 120 m (City news of 16 Jul 2025 [R31], RWR 'about 120 m'); not reconciled. None of the four new sources gives an as-built level, crest survey, section or seabed depth, so the 3D model's seabed and heights are unchanged (LOW). A 70,000 t sensitivity is in the 3D model (design outline: 37,898 m3, mean height 2.89 m) [3d/METHODS_3D.md].
cost: City of Albany 'Total Committed Funds' AUD $11.75 million; Wikipedia/ABC/Beachgrit report project cost as approximately AUD $13 million [R3][R1][R7]
cost_usd_approx: ~USD $7.6-8.5 million at an approximate, unsourced AUD->USD conversion of ~0.65-0.72 (indicative only, not independently sourced) [R3][R1][R7] ASSUMPTION A1: the AUD->USD factor 0.65-0.72 is the agent's rough recollection, no exchange-rate source consulted (replace with the RBA rate for 2024-25); effect about +-10 %.
financed_by: Commonwealth (Australian) Government $4.75M; WA State Government (DPIRD) $5M; City of Albany $1.995M; Albany Boardriders club $5,000 [R3]. CONFLICT: the City page lists Commonwealth 4.75 M and WA 5 M; the WA Government statement of 14 Jan 2025 ('Cook Government is contributing $4.75 million') and Raised Water Research give WA 4.75 M and Commonwealth 5 M [R32][R10]; not resolved (the total is the same). WA state pledge from both major parties in the 2017 election; federal pledge from both major parties in 2022 [R3][R2][R6]
motivation: Middleton Beach produced 'unreliable and unsurfable waves for much of the year' despite being closest to central Albany; ~30 years of local-surfer advocacy (led by Peter Bolt from 1990) sought a consistent, surfable wave to build youth surf access, tourism, and economic development for Albany - not a response to erosion or a port-mitigation problem [R1][R6][R3][R8]
designer: Bluecoast Consulting Engineers, lead design engineer Evan Watterson (principal engineer at Bluecoast per the firm's own bio; 'Principal Coastal Engineer / Director' per a separate CV) [R3][R16]
contractor: Heron Construction Limited (main contractor; marine personnel crew mobilised from New Zealand); Stantec (project superintendent); Spinifex Crushing & Screening Services (rock supplier, quarry at Mindijup Rd, Palmdale); marine plant (backhoe dredge, barges/tugs) mobilised via Darwin and Adelaide [R3][R2][R6][R17]
status_now: Built and operating since July 2025 [R1][R2]. About 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days in late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026) by commercial divers with a local vessel and Albany Boardriders, at 'more than $20,000' (lede) or 'about $24,000' (City estimate), in response to a spate of user injuries [R3][R11][R8] Decision: verdict 'mixed' was assigned by the dossier agent (verified_on 2026-09-24), not by a source: wave quality is reported as a success [R2][R8][R10], but injuries led to a proposed detuning and a rock repositioning [R7][R11], and no monitoring data exist. The repositioning cost is from one paywalled article only (two figures in it: >20,000 and about 24,000; read from the page metadata, no login, see D12).
hover_text: 165 m long, 62,800-tonne rock reef built for AUD ~$13M (opened July 2025) that delivers a widely praised, better-than-design surf break - but its shallow, permeable rock crest caused repeated surfer injuries, forcing an 18-rock, $20,000+ safety 'detuning' in March 2026 [R1][R2][R3][R11].
design_as_planned: The 2015 Feasibility Study's objective was 'the creation of a consistent, surfable wave, which maximises available swell conditions' for Albany's economic and demographic benefit [R3]. The Detailed Design (executive summary by 2020) targeted a left-hand break, rides up to 100 m, and surfable waves 41% of the year, aimed at beginner-to-intermediate surfers per EPA WA [R3][R2][R9]. Design used 'thorough numerical, physical and conceptual modelling', with a 2018 BMT Environmental Impact Assessment, read at the source in October 2026: its shoreline-modelling appendix says 'In all the simulations tested, there appeared to be a widening of the shoreline' (PDF p.151) and the report expects offshore placement to give no significant shoreline impact compared with inshore placement (PDF p.38) [R20]; these findings were earlier cited via [R3][R8]. Business-case modelling projected NPV $57.9M / BCR 6.69, driven by ~10 annual surfing events and ~3,500 extra overnight visitors/year (an earlier May-2023 interim figure gave NPV $19.4M / BCR 3.25) [R3][R15].
as_built_vs_design: The built reef matches the design specification closely on paper: 165 m long, up to 110 m wide, crest at -1.0 m AHD, 62,800 t of rock in three graded layers [R3]. Construction: quarry from ~Oct 2024 [R17]; first rock on the seabed 18 Mar 2025, planned six weeks [R26][R30]; 'more than two-thirds complete' on 16 May 2025 with finish moved to mid-June [R27]; opened 16 Jul 2025 [R29][R31] (the earlier reading 'main placement Jan-Mar 2025, practical completion Mar 2025' came from the City's programme and the WA Government statement of 14 Jan 2025, which were plans [R3][R32]). A New Zealand marine crew used precision geospatial placement equipment [R3][R2][R8]. Storm of Mon 26 May 2025 (highest waves in King George Sound since 2017) moved some of the smaller CORE rock shoreward before the armour was on top; the contractor surveyed and replaced it before opening [R25][R28]. No as-built level, crest survey, section or seabed depth has been published (checked again 2026-10-13 in four new sources). Once open, the reef performed 'far higher' than the 41% design-surfability target [R2][R6], though no source gives a precise revised percentage (Raised Water Research gives about 40 % of the year breaking on the reef proper [R10], which does not support 'far higher'; the claim rests on quotes in R2/R6 only). The most significant post-opening change came in late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026): about 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days by commercial divers with a local vessel and Albany Boardriders, after surveys in late 2025; cost 'more than $20,000' in the article lede and 'about $24,000' as the City's estimate (paywalled article, text read from the page metadata) [R11][R18]. This is a later change: the 3D model shows the 2025 design state, and this goes in as a note, not as geometry.
outcome: Widely reported as a rare unambiguous artificial-surf-reef success on wave quality: Swellnet says 'the reef performs far better than expectations' [R8]; Peter Bolt calls it 'intermediate-to-advanced on most days' as swell grows [R6][R2]; local surfer Cameron Warburton calls it 'a really high-performance wave' [R2]. Raised Water Research describes 0.8-1.3 m faces, 100-120 m rides, breaking on the reef proper ~40% of the year [R10]. But a persistent forum question (Aug-Oct 2025, user 'steveb') is whether it breaks well on the small (<1 m) everyday swells that dominate the local climate; local 'soggydog' answered 'No, but it has created reliable banks either side when it's too small for the reef proper' [R8]. No monitoring data, beach-width surveys, storm-damage, or fisheries/ecology results were found in sources fetched, beyond the single 2018 EIA citation [R8].
why_worked_or_failed: Sources attribute the reef's relative success to layered, precision-placed rock construction rather than geotextile sand bags, which 'failed due to the bags splitting, shifting, or settling' at earlier reefs worldwide [R8][R3][R6]. Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) argues rock reefs cannot match a sand-formed bank's contour accuracy because armour rock must be massive for stability, so shallow enough placement to break small swells 'compromises user safety'; rock permeability also means small swells 'surge into the reef rather than shoal and break', while larger swells ride over imperfections and shoal further up - explaining why the reef performs much better on bigger swells [R8]. He contrasts Albany's shallow crest (-1.0 m AHD, chosen partly 'to maximise wave breaking') unfavourably with Palm Beach (Gold Coast), which mitigated injury risk with a deeper crest [R8][R3]. Mayor Greg Stocks frames the injuries more as a behavioural issue: 'inexperienced surfers taking on quite elite waves...the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that' [R7].
unexpected_results: Injuries began within weeks of opening: Swellnet forum posts from Albany locals describe 'a good face injury', sharp rocks cutting feet, and (per 'Baldhead') 'a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion' [R8]. By October 2025 the reef was being considered for 'detuning' ('busting up a couple of the rocks in the shallower part of the wave') following a 'spate of injuries on beginner surfers who can't handle its juice' [R7]. In late February 2026 (reported 11 March 2026) about 18 'high rocks' were repositioned over two days, at 'more than $20,000' (lede) / 'about $24,000' (City estimate) [R11][R18]. Earlier, the storm of 26 May 2025 had already moved some core rock shoreward during construction [R25][R28]. 'steveb' argued this represented a public-liability/facility-design failure, comparing the reef to a council-managed playground where 'public safety is the number one priority' [R8]. Positive unplanned effects include reliable secondary sand-bank breaks either side of the reef on small swells, and youth/community access described by Peter Bolt watching 'the kids come down here before school, in the dark, to get a wave before they go to school' [R8][R2]. Shark risk is raised as a live community concern (no confirmed incident found) [R8].
could_be_better: Engineer 'steveb' (Swellnet) proposes that rock-dumped reefs inherently trade wave-shape accuracy against user safety, and argues a fully prefabricated reef structure - built onshore, floated out, and installed by controlled submergence - could achieve 'accurate shape and level, no subsidence, no settlement, no sharp edges, no possible entrapment points', citing materials with a 'safe working life in excess of 100 years', and points to Palm Beach's deeper, safer crest as a precedent for the safety/wave-quality trade-off Albany did not take [R8][R3]. Most surfer sentiment in the sources is not calling for a safer/easier wave - several posters push back on 'detuning' as inherent to a legitimately world-class wave - but there is a recurring, unanswered request for clearer information on how reliably the reef breaks on the small, sub-1 m swells that make up most of Middleton Beach's actual wave climate [R7][R8].
relevance_to_israel: King George Sound (Albany) is micro-tidal (mean range 0.4 m, spring 1.1 m), broadly comparable to the Mediterranean at Haifa, which is also effectively micro-tidal, though no fetched source gives a numeric Haifa tidal-range figure [R5][R10]. Official Albany figures differ in form from the Wikipedia ones: the 2018 BMT assessment gives a Middleton Beach spring range of 0.9 m and a neap range of 0.3 m, largest range below 1.5 m [R20]; the WA Department of Transport / Bureau of Meteorology predictions for 2024 run from 0.12 to 1.40 m above LAT, mean 0.742 m above LAT (1,043 high and low waters) [R22]. Datums and averaging periods differ, so the figures are not reconciled. Albany's wave climate (consistent, long-period 12-16s Southern Ocean groundswell) is fundamentally more energetic than Haifa's, where Lior's own Shikmona-buoy measurements define 'minimum surfable' at only 0.45-0.6 m within a narrow WNW swell window [R10][R12]; the 6-8 s period is NOT part of his buoy-based definition: in his notes it belongs to the '4Surfers' forecast-site cross-check (page 1) [R12], while the periods he read off the buoy charts are 5.7-6.2 s (pages 3-4, 6 and 15 Aug 2025) [R12]. Albany's problem was reshaping abundant swell into a rideable, non-closeout wave; Haifa/Israel's problem is swell scarcity ('less than 1 day/week' naturally surfable per Lior's Haifa proposal) [R13]. What transfers: (1) rock-vs-geotextile construction lesson; (2) the shallow-crest/wave-quality vs deeper-crest/safety trade-off any Haifa project would also face; (3) the multi-decade, multi-level-government (federal/state/city/club) financing pattern; (4) because Haifa is swell-starved rather than closeout-prone, Albany is a better precedent for safe rock-reef engineering than for wave-energy requirements, where Lior's own Gold Coast/Narrowneck comparison may be more directly analogous [R8][R3][R13].

reviews.role: long-time Albany surfer, lead advocate for ~30 years
reviews.quote_or_summary: We just felt that's where we needed the juniors to have something decent to surf... in town where they can get access to it.
It's a really high-performance wave, and the reef is creating a culture around town that's really good.

reviews.role: self-identified Albany local, Swellnet forum poster
reviews.quote_or_summary: Visitor had a good face injury yesterday. The rocks are sharp, feet are pretty cut up... It's not a beginner wave. There are dangers. But it's pretty fucking epic when you get a good one.
There's been a number of injuries - broken bones, gashes, concussion. There's a hardy crew on it.
Well done Albany council! Proper tubey take-off, big open face section to carve off too... Good vibes in the line-up too (for now anyhow).
Mixed report: on a given swell 'it didn't seem to be breaking very well, quite full and inconsistent,' while nearby beach breaks were closing out well that day.

reviews.role: Swellnet forum poster, self-identified public-recreation-facility engineer
reviews.quote_or_summary: The potential for far more serious injuries seems high... can artificial surfing reefs be made safer and better?
A much-loved local asset and a source of pride for surfers, families and the wider community, crediting passion, persistence and community support.

[The surf reef] does perform very well at different times, and the temptation to go there above your skill level is probably contributing to some of that... surfers acknowledge that there's risk, and all the surfing community that I've spoken to are delighted with the surf reef.
